Cell cycle and cancer

Why HeLa keeps dividing

An immortal cell line can keep producing new generations when given the right conditions in a lab. Individual HeLa cells can still die.

Watch a HeLa culture grow

Start with two cells. Watch parent cells round up, separate into daughters, and spread into open space. The model ends with 20 cells after 10 rounds of staggered divisions.

Starting culture 2 cells

The animation compresses time and uses an even layout so each division is easy to see. A successful division adds one cell to the total.

Compare two cell cultures

Start

Many ordinary cultured cells

HeLa cell line

Both cultures start with a small group of cells.

This illustration compares patterns over time. The dots and steps are not measured counts or times.

Chromosome ends

Telomeres protect the tips of chromosomes. They often shorten as ordinary cells divide. HeLa cells have active telomerase, an enzyme that helps maintain those tips.

Growth checkpoints

HeLa cells carry DNA from HPV type 18. The viral proteins E6 and E7 interfere with growth control pathways involving p53 and Rb. Telomerase and altered growth controls both help explain why the line can keep dividing.

Henrietta Lacks

The cells came from her cervical tumor in 1951 and were used for research without her knowledge or consent. HeLa is a cancer cell line used in laboratories. Read about her legacy at NIH.

BIOL 1406 and research sources

Connect this lesson to cell cycle checkpoints and cancer and the cell cycle. See ATCC’s HeLa cell line record and the study on telomerase and growth arrest in HeLa.

The 3D animation draws on time-lapse studies of HeLa cell lineages, cell rounding before mitosis, and daughter cells spreading after division.

Cell structure

Interphase

This cell is spread out on the surface where it grows. Its nucleus is intact. During interphase the cell does its usual work and copies its DNA before division.

Anatomy in this view

Which structure controls what enters and leaves?

The plasma membrane.

Microscopy-inspired teaching models. Colors, structures and motion are simplified. Enlarged for viewing. The animation compresses the timing and shows a representative subset of chromosomes.

The dissolves illustrate structures losing their organized shape. Nuclear membrane material redistributes into the ER, and Golgi fragments, mitochondria, and peroxisomes are passed on to the daughter cells.

About the cell and its sources

HeLa is an immortal human cancer cell line that began with cells from Henrietta Lacks’s cervical tumor in 1951. The cells were used for research without her knowledge or consent. NIH: Henrietta Lacks and HeLa

Model references: NIGMS fluorescence microscopy, Wellcome metaphase microscopy, Wellcome cytokinesis microscopy, and Janelia whole-cell volume atlas. Course reference: OpenStax, The Cell Cycle.
